meta.title: Who really said "Half of what I say is meaningless, but I say it so that the other half may reach you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it is Kahlil Gibran — from Sand and Foam (Alfred A. Knopf, 1926). The book prints a semicolon; John Lennon reworked the line for the Beatles in 1968.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Half of what I say is meaningless, but I say it so that the other half may reach you'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Gibran: the line is in Sand and Foam (Knopf, 1926), written in English. Original punctuation is a semicolon; Lennon adapted it for 'Julia' (1968).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence appears as a freestanding aphorism in Gibran’s Sand and Foam: A Book of Aphorisms, first published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1926 — and Gibran wrote it in English, so there is no translator standing between you and the wording. The book prints it with a semicolon: “Half of what I say is meaningless; but I say it so that the other half may reach you.”

source.excerpt:
The reality of the other person is not in what he reveals to you, but in what he cannot reveal to you. Therefore, if you would understand him, listen not to what he says but rather to what he does not say.

Half of what I say is meaningless; but I say it so that the other half may reach you.
trail: Wikisource’s complete text of Sand and Foam ↗ contains the sentence verbatim and reproduces the book’s copyright page: “COPYRIGHT, 1926, BY KAHLIL GIBRAN”, Alfred A. Knopf.
A second, independent transcription at Project Gutenberg Australia ↗ gives identical wording and punctuation, and places the line immediately after the aphorism about what a person cannot reveal.
The 1926 Knopf first edition is cataloged and scanned: Internet Archive ↗ and Open Library ↗ both record A.A. Knopf, New York, 1926, 85 pages, LCCN 26019300.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Sand and Foam (1926) among its sourced quotations — not in the Misattributed section.
source.excerptNote: The two aphorisms run consecutively in the book, in the order shown — confirmed against both the Wikisource and Project Gutenberg Australia transcriptions. Note the semicolon; the version that circulates online usually swaps in a comma.

source.rightsNote: Sand and Foam was first published in the United States in 1926, and US works published that long ago are now in the public domain — the Academy of American Poets says so plainly when reprinting the book, noting “These poems are in the public domain” ↗ for the Knopf 1926 text. The 1926 notice was renewed in 1954 by the Gibran estate, but that renewal term has since run out, which is why Wikisource and Project Gutenberg Australia can host the complete text. No translation copyright applies: Gibran wrote the book in English.

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: About Kahlil Gibran
author.metaLine: 1883–1931 · Lebanese-American poet and artist, author of The Prophet (1923)
author.bio: Gibran was born in Bsharri, in what is now Lebanon, on 6 January 1883, and emigrated with his mother and siblings to Boston in 1895. He wrote his early work in Arabic and most of his post-1918 work in English, a switch that produced The Prophet (1923) — one of the best-selling books of the century — and its terser companion volume, Sand and Foam (1926). He died in New York City on 10 April 1931.

misattribution.heading: Wording drift and the Beatles detour
misattribution.intro: Nobody credible steals this one from Gibran — it is his, and the sourced references agree. What goes wrong is smaller and stickier: the punctuation changes in transit, and a great many people first meet the sentence as a rock lyric rather than as a 1926 aphorism.

items.why: Both independent full texts of the book — Wikisource ↗ and Project Gutenberg Australia ↗ — print a semicolon after “meaningless”. The form that circulates online, including on Wikiquote ↗ and the aggregator sites, uses a comma. Same sentence, softer joint; the semicolon is what Knopf set in 1926.

Lennon opened “Julia” on The Beatles (1968) with a close rewrite of this line. Wikipedia describes his lyric as “a slight variation” of the Sand and Foam sentence ↗, and notes he adapted other Gibran material for the same song. Lennon never passed it off as his own idea, but the song is how the sentence reached most of its audience — which is why it sometimes gets filed under 1968 rather than 1926.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is genuinely Gibran’s, written in English and printed in Sand and Foam (Alfred A. Knopf, 1926) ↗ — semicolon and all.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Sand and Foam came three years after The Prophet, and it is a very different kind of book: no narrator, no frame story, just a run of unnumbered aphorisms and parables, some a paragraph long and some a single sentence. Gibran wrote it in English and illustrated it himself. The form is the point — each line has to survive on its own, without any surrounding argument to prop it up.

This particular aphorism is a writer’s confession of method. It sits directly after a longer entry about how a person’s reality lives in what they cannot say, which makes the sequence read as a single thought: language mostly fails, so you keep talking and let the odds do the rest. That is a strikingly modest thing to find in a book usually shelved under inspirational wisdom.
detailsBody: Because Sand and Foam is a book of unnumbered aphorisms rather than numbered verses, citations to it usually name the book and year rather than a page. We have not verified a page number against the 1926 first edition, so we do not assert one.
context.pull: Language mostly fails — so you keep talking and let the odds do the rest.

sourcesVerified.claim: The complete text of Sand and Foam contains "Half of what I say is meaningless; but I say it so that the other half may reach you." and reproduces the 1926 Alfred A. Knopf copyright page (COPYRIGHT, 1926, BY KAHLIL GIBRAN; renewal 1954 by the Gibran estate).

An independent full text of Sand and Foam contains the identical sentence with a semicolon, immediately following the aphorism "The reality of the other person is not in what he reveals to you..." and immediately preceding "A sense of humour is a sense of proportion."

Wikiquote lists the line under Sand and Foam (1926) in its sourced quotes section, not under Misattributed or Disputed, and notes John Lennon paraphrased it in "Julia" (1968). Wikiquote renders the line with a comma rather than a semicolon.

The article states that Lennon's opening line in "Julia" was "a slight variation" of Kahlil Gibran's Sand and Foam (1926), whose original verse reads "Half of what I say is meaningless, but I say it so that the other half may reach you", and that Lennon adapted further lines from Gibran for the song.

Kahlil Gibran was born 6 January 1883 in Bsharri (present-day Lebanon), emigrated to the United States in 1895, wrote most of his post-1918 work in English, published The Prophet in 1923 and Sand and Foam in 1926, and died in New York City on 10 April 1931.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Sand and Foam; a book of aphorisms by Kahlil Gibran (1883-1931), published by A.A. Knopf, New York, 1926, 85 pages, LCCN 26019300.
The Open Library catalog record gives Sand and foam: a book of aphorisms by Kahlil Gibran, A.A. Knopf, New York, 1926, 85 pages, LCCN 26019300, OCLC 1075853.

The Academy of American Poets reprints selections from Sand and Foam and states: "From Sand and Foam by Kahlil Gibran (Alfred A. Knopf, 1926). These poems are in the public domain." (This page does NOT itself contain the "Half of what I say" aphorism; it is cited only for the edition and public-domain statement.)
A third transcription of Sand and Foam prints the sentence with a semicolon: "Half of what I say is meaningless; but I say it so that the other half may reach you."
A quotation aggregator attributes the line to Kahlil Gibran's Sand and Foam (1926) but with a comma instead of a semicolon, and supplies no page number or edition detail.
